headline: SK Hynix forecasts 2027 to be 'worst year' for memory shortage, crunch expected until 2030
summary: SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung shared this grim outlook on the day the company marked the largest-ever IPO for a foreign company on the U.S. stock market, raising $26.5 billion.
details: SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung has stated that 2027 will be the "worst year" for the ongoing memory shortage, with the crunch expected to last until 2030. This forecast was made as SK Hynix completed a record-breaking $26.5 billion IPO on Nasdaq.

Kwak emphasized that customer demand is projected to remain higher than supply capacity even beyond 2030, despite the company's efforts to address the issue. This aligns with previous statements from SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won.

The primary driver for DRAM demand is High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) used in AI accelerators. HBM requires more sophisticated manufacturing and packaging processes, consuming significantly more wafer capacity than consumer DDR5.

While such forecasts could benefit SK Hynix financially, the company has also been involved in long-term supply agreements (LTAs). These agreements commit supply over multiple years and define price floors and ceilings, securing demand for DRAM.

Despite the grim outlook, there have been some signs of the market cooling. A recent TrendForce report showed DRAM contract prices up 15% to 18% quarter-over-quarter for Q3 2026, a large increase but lower than previous QoQ jumps.

The memory market is nearing a form of stability, albeit at elevated prices. However, market trends can change rapidly, as seen with the recent pivot towards AI spending on CPUs, which boosted Intel's stock while impacting Nvidia's market cap.
